result.summary: The landlord approved the bedroom radiator repair on two conditions: Harlow Heating only, and no more than £150. Neither option we have meets both. Harlow is fully booked until 3 November, and its sooner emergency visit is double rate and not priced. Quick Fix Heating quoted £230 and is not the named firm. I asked the landlord to choose between three options and gave the tenant safe checks to try and an update. Nothing is booked, and a hold is in place to follow up in 2 days.

judgement.why_this_decision: Event 003 is a conditional approval: Harlow only, £150 maximum, ask before spending more. The classifier also read it as conditional_approval, with only 0.02 chance of being unconditional. Event 004: Harlow can't do a standard visit before 3 November, and an emergency visit is double rate. Event 005: Quick Fix quoted £230, which is £80 over the cap and not the firm the landlord named. Neither option is within the landlord's authority, and only the landlord can decide, so I asked them. This is not a safety emergency: one room is affected, the rest of the house heats normally, and no vulnerability has been recorded. So I didn't dispatch anyone without approval.

alternatives_considered.option: Assign Quick Fix for Monday 6 October
alternatives_considered.why_not: The landlord explicitly said Harlow only and £150 maximum. £230 is over the cap and the firm isn't the landlord's choice.
It is double rate and unpriced, so it would probably go over £150 without the landlord's say-so.

alternatives_considered.option: Wait for Harlow's standard slot without asking
alternatives_considered.why_not: The tenant would have a freezing room for about a month. The landlord should make that trade-off knowingly.
The landlord can resolve this directly. I'll escalate if there's no reply after follow-up or if the tenant reports vulnerability.
The classifier's emergency probability was only 0.43. Heating works in the rest of the house and no vulnerability is known, so I asked the tenant about vulnerability instead.
